sections.h2: Who bills and collects property tax
sections.html:
In New Hampshire the city or town does all of it. Each municipality assesses the property, sets the rate and collects the money under RSA 76 and the Rev 600 rules. The state does not send homeowners a bill. The Department of Revenue Administration (DRA) watches assessing practices, reviews municipal records and oversees revaluations, but it is not who you pay.

When you sell, you will deal with two local offices. The assessor answers value questions. The tax collector gives payoff figures and tells you whether a lien exists. Two houses that sell for the same price in neighboring towns can carry very different bills, because each town picks its own rate.

The property tax year runs from April 1 to March 31 (RSA 76:2), and taxes are based on the inventory taken in April. A fall sale does not change that: the April 1 assessment still drives the bills that arrive afterward, so work out the split with your closing attorney or title company before you sign.

Towns and cities that bill twice a year follow RSA 76:15-a. A partial payment is due July 1 and the balance is due December 1.

  • The July bill is built from the prior year's assessed value times one-half of the previous year's tax rate.
  • Assessors commit the lists to the collector by May 15, and the partial-payment bills go out no later than June 15.
  • The December bill is whatever remains of the taxes assessed April 1, minus the July payment.

Not every municipality uses that pattern. Concord, for one, sends four quarterly bills in July, October, January and March, based on the prior April 1 assessment. The due dates printed on your own bill are the ones that count, so read it or call your collector.

Interest runs at 8 percent per annum on taxes not paid by December 1 after assessment (RSA 76:13). Hampton's town page describes the same 8 percent rate, counted daily from the day after a bill is due.

sections.h2: What happens if the taxes are not paid?
sections.html:
An unpaid bill can turn into a tax lien, and a lien nobody redeems can end in a tax deed. This is the collection chapter, RSA 80, and it applies in municipalities that use the lien procedure.

  • The collector must send notice of the impending lien at least 30 days before executing it, by certified or registered mail, return receipt requested (RSA 80:60).
  • Only the municipality, the county or the state can hold a tax lien on land and buildings (RSA 80:63).
  • Anyone with a legal interest in the land can redeem by paying the lien amount plus interest at 14 percent per annum from the execution date, at any point before the collector gives a deed (RSA 80:69).
  • Once 2 years pass from execution of an unredeemed lien, the collector executes a tax deed to the lienholder (RSA 80:76).

The jump from 8 to 14 percent is where owners start to feel real pressure. If you are behind and thinking about selling, plan on the redemption payment coming out of your proceeds at closing. A municipality may also refuse a tax deed, in which case the lien stays in place and the right of redemption continues.

Begin with a written abatement application to your town's selectmen or assessors. The deadline is March 1 after the date on your notice of tax (RSA 76:16), and the form comes from the Board of Tax and Land Appeals (BTLA). You must have complied with the RSA 74 inventory requirement, and the application has to give specific reasons and list any comparable properties. A vague complaint about the amount rarely goes anywhere, so bring numbers.

Abatement and appeal deadlines
StepDeadline
Apply for abatement with the municipalityMarch 1 after the notice of tax
Municipality decides in writingJuly 1 after the notice of tax date; no response counts as denial
Appeal to BTLA, notice of tax on or before Dec. 31September 1, but no earlier than the municipal decision or July 1
Appeal to BTLA, notice of tax after Dec. 318 months after the notice of tax
BTLA filing fee$65, check or money order to Treasurer, State of NH

An abatement is a request for a refund of taxes because of a physical description error, damage to a building during the tax year, or a difference of opinion on value. If the town turns you down, the next step can be an appeal to BTLA or to Superior Court.

New Hampshire offers several exemptions and military-service credits, and nothing is applied unless the owner asks. The permanent application, Form PA-29, goes to the municipal assessing officials by April 15, before the tax rate is set. They respond by July 1. No response counts as a denial, which can be appealed to BTLA or Superior Court by September 1 after the notice of tax.

  • Elderly exemption (RSA 72:39-a): the applicant must be 65 by April 1 and a New Hampshire resident for three consecutive years, and income and asset limits apply.
  • Blind exemption (RSA 72:37): $15,000 off the assessed value unless the town votes more.
  • Standard service credit (RSA 72:28): $50 standard, and towns can adopt $51 up to $750.
  • Service-connected total disability credit (RSA 72:35): $700 standard, and towns can adopt up to $5,000.
  • Disabled exemption (RSA 72:37-b): only where the town has adopted it.

The qualifying date is April 1 of the tax year. Exemptions belong to a person and a home, so a buyer applies for their own. If you sell and move before the next April 1, ask the assessing office how that affects any credit you hold.

Before closing day, find out from the tax collector exactly what is owed, including any lien amount. Ask for a written payoff figure and for confirmation of whether a lien has been executed on the parcel.

  • Pull your most recent bill, and the previous year's if any part is unpaid.
  • Ask whether a notice of impending lien has been sent, and when interest started.
  • If a lien exists, ask for the redemption amount through the expected closing date, since interest at 14 percent per annum keeps running.
  • Plan for the transfer tax: $.75 per $100 of the price from the seller and the same from the buyer, paid with stamps bought from the register of deeds.

When back taxes, a lien and needed repairs all pile up, an as-is cash sale can be a cleaner way out, because the buyer does not wait on a lender's appraisal. No price or timeline is promised here. Talk with your collector and a New Hampshire attorney for your exact numbers.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: Your city or town does. Municipalities assess, levy and collect under RSA 76, and the state Department of Revenue Administration monitors assessing practices.

faqs.q: When are New Hampshire property taxes due?
faqs.a: In towns that bill twice a year, a partial payment is due July 1 and the balance December 1. Some municipalities bill quarterly, so follow the dates printed on your own bill.

faqs.q: What interest applies to late property taxes?
faqs.a: Eight percent per annum on taxes not paid by December 1 after assessment (RSA 76:13). After a lien is executed, redemption carries 14 percent per annum (RSA 80:69).

faqs.q: What is the deadline to ask for an abatement?
faqs.a: March 1 following the date of the notice of tax. The municipality must decide in writing by July 1, and no response is a denial. The BTLA filing fee is $65.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house that has a tax lien?
faqs.a: Yes. A person with a legal interest can redeem by paying the lien amount plus 14 percent per annum before the collector gives a deed, and in a sale that payoff is usually handled from the proceeds at closing.
